items.prompt: What is defense in depth?
choices: Independent layers, each assuming the last one failed
One very strong control placed right at the network edge
The same check copied several times in a row
items.explanation: Independent controls stack, so one failure is not total compromise.

items.prompt: Why are three identical locks not three layers?
choices: Locks only work one at a time
Identical locks cost more to install
Whatever opens one opens all three
items.explanation: Identical locks share the same weakness, so beating one beats them all.

items.prompt: Each layer in a stack is built on which assumption?
choices: The layer before it is guaranteed to hold in practice
The layer before it may already have been bypassed
Nobody will ever attack it
items.explanation: Each layer is designed for the day the previous one fails.

items.prompt: Castle A's thief opened all twelve rooms with one key. What was missing?
choices: Separate locks, so one key opens only one room
A taller and thicker wall around the whole castle
A louder alarm bell hung beside the front gate
items.explanation: Separate locks per room would have limited the key to a single room.

items.prompt: A second firewall running the very same rules adds mostly what?
choices: A new kind of check
Redundancy, not a new kind of check
Protection against stolen keys
items.explanation: The same rules ask the same question, so the second firewall is a copy.

items.prompt: Which layer asks a different question from a payload scanner?
choices: A scoped account asking if the credential can do this at all
A second scanner built on exactly the same list of attack patterns
A third scanner from another vendor with similar patterns
items.explanation: Only the scoped account asks about the credential rather than the payload.

items.prompt: Which question do authentication and authorization alone NOT answer?
choices: Who is making this request?
Is this person allowed to do this thing?
What can a breached component reach next?
items.explanation: Both run per request. Containing a breached component is a design-time question.

items.prompt: Why does a stack of imperfect layers still help?
choices: Each layer makes the earlier layers behave perfectly
An attacker must pass every one, so the odds multiply down
Imperfect layers quietly cancel out one another's mistakes
items.explanation: Pass rates multiply, so each extra independent layer cuts the odds sharply.

items.prompt: What is a credential's blast radius?
choices: The damage a stolen credential could cause
How many characters the password contains in total
The number of people who know the password
items.explanation: Blast radius is the damage a stolen or misused credential can do.

items.prompt: What does least privilege give a service account?
choices: Every permission, in case it is needed later
Only the access its job needs
The same access as the person who created it
items.explanation: Least privilege means the minimum the job requires.

items.prompt: Which kind of account did Meridian's web server hold?
choices: A read-only account on two tables
No database account at all
A shared admin account
items.explanation: Meridian used one admin account for convenience.

items.prompt: Why does 'just use admin' keep happening?
choices: Scoping takes effort, and admin takes the least
Databases require an admin account for every service
Scoped accounts are not supported by databases
items.explanation: Admin is the path of least effort, which is the opposite of least privilege.

items.prompt: What could Castellan's web account do?
choices: Select, insert, update, delete, and drop on 47 tables
Select on 2 tables
Select on all 47 tables
items.explanation: It was scoped to select on exactly two non-sensitive tables.

items.prompt: A service only reads one table. Which account fits best?
choices: One that can select from every table
One that can do anything on that table
One that can only select from that table
items.explanation: Least privilege matches both the table and the operation to the need.

items.prompt: Is least privilege a one-time setting?
choices: No, it must be revisited as the service changes
Yes, set it once at launch and forget it
Yes, but only for admin accounts
items.explanation: Needs change, and wide scopes added under pressure need pulling back.

items.prompt: A grant covers 2 tables averaging 4,270 records each. How many records are exposed?
What does zero trust mean?
choices: No request is trusted for its origin alone
Nobody is ever allowed to log in anywhere
Only requests from outside the network are checked
items.explanation: Every request is verified on its own merits, whatever its origin.

items.prompt: Where does castle-and-moat put its serious checks?
choices: On every call between internal services
At the edge of the network
Only inside the database
items.explanation: The perimeter does the checking; the inside is treated as trusted.

items.prompt: In a castle-and-moat network, calls between internal services are usually...
choices: Checked twice as strictly
Blocked unless approved by hand
Trusted without being re-checked
items.explanation: Inside the walls, services tend to trust each other by default.

items.prompt: Under zero trust, should two services in the same cluster check each other?
choices: Yes, on every request
No, the cluster is trusted
Only the first time they connect
items.explanation: Zero trust does not cache trust from network position.

items.prompt: What did Meridian lack inside its perimeter?
choices: A firewall at the front door of the network
A check between its own internal parts
A login page for customers
items.explanation: It had edge controls but nothing between its own internal parts.

items.prompt: Which are the two questions in a zero-trust check?
choices: How fast is the call, and how big is it?
Where is the call from, and when was it sent?
Who is calling, and may they do this?
items.explanation: Identity and permission are checked separately on every request.

items.prompt: Which idea bounds how easily anything becomes trusted at all?
choices: Zero trust
Least privilege
Encryption at rest
items.explanation: Least privilege limits what trusted components can do. Zero trust limits who gets trusted.

items.prompt: Does being on the internal network show a caller is legitimate?
choices: Yes, because outsiders cannot get in
No, a breached component is also inside
Yes, if the firewall is up to date
items.explanation: A taken-over component sits inside the network just like a legitimate one.

items.prompt: Which layer stops a stolen password when no route to the database exists?
choices: Network policy
Monitoring
Encryption at rest
items.explanation: With no route, the password cannot be used from that host at all.

items.prompt: A scoped account stops an attacker who legitimately reached the database tier from what?
choices: Reaching the proxy
Reading tables outside its grant
Calling other services
items.explanation: The route is allowed, but the grant limits which tables can be read.

items.prompt: After default-deny is applied, what does a NetworkPolicy allow?
choices: Everything until a rule denies it
Only web pods
Nothing until a rule allows it
items.explanation: Default-deny starts closed and opens only named paths.

items.prompt: Which port does Castellan's web tier use to reach the proxy?
items.explanation: Web egress allows the proxy on port 8443. The database listens on 5432.

items.prompt: Which layer shortens how long a quiet breach goes unnoticed?
choices: Network segmentation
Monitoring and alerting
Least-privilege accounts
items.explanation: Monitoring is what notices permitted-but-suspicious activity.

items.prompt: What does a single-hop blast-radius count include?
choices: Every service in the whole company, every table
Only restricted data
Only the compromised component's own grants
items.explanation: It adds up that component's direct grants and nothing beyond.

items.prompt: Why is the Meridian row in the blast-radius table so large?
choices: Its account reaches every table
Its server was slower
Its attacker was more skilled
items.explanation: The grant, not the attacker, sets the number.

items.prompt: What does billing's per-request authorization stop?
choices: A stolen password replayed from outside the cluster network
An order service asking for data it was never granted
A disk being copied while the machine is powered off
items.explanation: The check applies the caller's own permission row, even for internal calls.

items.prompt: A bank puts three firewalls from the same vendor in a row, all running identical rules. What did it gain?
choices: Redundancy against device failure, not depth: one rule gap passes all three
True depth, because an attacker must defeat three separate devices in turn, one after another
Nothing at all, because extra devices only ever add latency without any benefit
Depth only if the three devices are placed in different buildings of the company
items.explanation: Identical rules ask one question three times. The devices help if one breaks, but a single rule gap passes all of them.
items.reference:
Layers versus copies
same question asked twice: redundancy
different question per layer: depth
each layer assumes the one before it failed
3 independent layers at 60% stop rate each: 6.4% get through
Why: an attacker must beat different checks in turn, so one blind spot cannot open every door.
items.learnMore:
Defense in depth

A layer earns its place by asking a different question from the layers around it. Independent layers multiply: if each stops an attacker 60% of the time, three of them let only 6.4% through. That arithmetic only holds when one weakness cannot defeat several layers at once.

Common mistake

Counting copies of the same control as extra layers. Two scanners with overlapping signatures share a blind spot.
items.reflection: Think of something you protect in daily life with more than one safeguard. Do the safeguards ask different questions, or the same one twice?

items.prompt: Which pair of controls is genuinely independent in the sense this unit uses?
choices: Two web application firewalls scanning for the same attack signatures
SHA-256 hashing of a password followed by SHA-256 hashing again
Network segmentation plus a scoped database account
A login check on one page repeated by an identical check on the next
items.explanation: Segmentation asks whether a route exists; the scoped account asks what the credential can do. Different questions, different failures.

items.prompt: A service reads 2 of the database's 47 tables. Which account is closest to least privilege?
choices: A dedicated account with select on exactly those 2 tables
The shared admin account, since it already covers both tables
A read-only account on all 47 tables, since reads cannot hurt
A dedicated account with every privilege on just those 2 tables
items.explanation: The right account matches both the tables and the operation. Reading everything or writing is more than the job needs.
items.reference:
Blast radius by account design
shared admin account: all 47 tables, read, write and drop
scoped web account: 2 tables, select only
stolen credential reaches exactly what it was granted
2 tables x 4,270 records (scenario average) = 8,540
Why: the grant decided before the breach sets the size of the damage after it.
items.learnMore:
Least privilege and blast radius

Least privilege asks what the smallest set of things is that can go wrong if this exact credential is stolen. That set is its blast radius, and it is set by what you grant, not by how the credential is stolen. Scoping is ongoing work, because needs and temptations to widen it keep changing.

Common mistake

Treating a scope as a one-time setting. Widening an account just for now rarely gets undone.
items.reflection: Think of a key, password, or permission you hold that is broader than what you actually use. What would it cost to narrow it?

items.prompt: At an average of 4,270 records per table, how many MORE records does a 47-table grant expose than a 3-table grant?
items.explanation: 47 x 4,270 = 200,690 and 3 x 4,270 = 12,810, so the difference is 187,880. The other values forget to subtract or miscount tables.

items.prompt: Service A, inside the cluster, calls service B. Under zero trust, what must B do?
choices: Verify A's identity and check A's permission for this exact request
Accept it, since the internal network already screened A
Accept it if A's address is inside the cluster's address range
Verify A once at startup, then trust it until the next restart
items.explanation: Zero trust re-checks identity and permission per request. Network position and cached trust are exactly what it refuses to rely on.
items.reference:
Castle-and-moat versus zero trust
castle and moat: serious checks at the edge, inside is trusted
zero trust: every request checked, wherever it came from
two questions per call: who is calling, and may they do this?
a breached component is inside the network too
Why: network location says where a packet arrived, not whether the caller is legitimate.
items.learnMore:
Zero trust

Zero trust treats being inside the network as meaningless on its own. Each service verifies the caller's identity and checks its permission for this request, every time. Meridian had a perimeter; what it lacked was any checkpoint inside it.

Common mistake

Reading zero trust as removing the firewall. The perimeter stays; it just stops being the only place trust is decided.
items.reflection: Think of a place where being inside is treated as proof you belong. What would change if each door asked you to prove it again?

Only traffic from outside the network is verified, since inside is safe

items.prompt: An attacker holds a valid database password, but the web tier has no network route to the database. Which layer stopped them?
choices: The network policy, which leaves no path for the password
The scoped database account, which lacks the needed grants
The monitoring system, which spotted the password in use
Encryption at rest, which scrambled the stored password
items.explanation: The password was valid, so account scoping never even ran. The missing route stopped the attempt.
items.reference:
Which layer stops which failure
stolen password, no route to the database: network policy
legitimate route, wrong table: scoped account
valid caller, wrong request: per-request authorization
allowed reads over weeks: monitoring and alerting
Why: each layer catches a failure the others pass, so skipping one leaves a real gap.
items.learnMore:
Failure modes and layers

Each realistic failure is stopped by a different layer. A stolen password is useless without a route, a legitimate route is limited by the account's grant, an internal caller is limited by its own permission row, and permitted-but-suspicious reading is caught by monitoring. A blast-radius count of direct grants is the first tool; multi-hop movement needs a graph walk.

Common mistake

Assuming one strong layer covers the others. The network policy does nothing about a legitimate route with an admin account behind it.
items.reflection: Think of a system you rely on that has several safeguards. Which failure does each one catch that the others would miss?

items.prompt: Implement `hasGrant(grants, table)`. `grants` maps table names to operation lists for one role, like `{ products: ["SELECT"] }`. Return `true` if the table is listed, otherwise `false`.
items.explanation: A table counts only when it has an operation list. Anything else, including a missing key, is false.

items.prompt: Implement `isReadOnly(operations)`. Return `true` when the list contains no operation other than `"SELECT"`.
items.explanation: Every operation must be SELECT. One write operation anywhere makes the grant more than read-only.

items.prompt: Implement `countTables(grants)`: how many tables a role's grants object lists.
items.explanation: Each key is one granted table, so the number of keys is the width of the grant.

items.prompt: Implement `isWide(grants, limit)`. Return `true` when the grants list MORE than `limit` tables.
items.explanation: The comparison is strictly greater than, so a grant exactly at the limit is not wide.

items.prompt: Implement `canSelect(operations)`. Return `true` only when the list includes `"SELECT"`.
items.explanation: An empty list grants nothing, so the answer is false. Only an explicit SELECT makes it true.

items.prompt: Implement `recordsExposed(counts, tables)`. `counts` maps table names to record counts. Return the total records across the listed `tables`; a table missing from `counts` adds 0.
items.explanation: Sum only the granted tables. The unlisted orders table never counts, and an unknown table contributes nothing.

items.prompt: Implement `canAccess(grants, role, table, operation)`. `grants` looks like `{ role: { table: ["SELECT", ...] } }`. Return `true` only if that role holds that exact operation on that exact table. Everything else, including an unknown role or table, is `false`.
items.explanation: The lookup returns undefined for an unknown role or table, and Array.isArray turns that into false. Only an explicit matching operation yields true, so the check fails closed.
items.reference:
Default-deny, written down
unknown role: deny
unlisted table: deny
listed table, wrong operation: deny
only an exact role, table, and operation match allows
Why: a forgotten rule then fails closed instead of open.
items.learnMore:
Fail closed

A permission check should answer yes only when it can point to a matching grant. Everything else, including missing roles, missing tables, and empty requests, falls through to no. The inverse design allows unless a deny rule matches, and fails open the first time someone forgets a rule.

Common mistake

Letting a missing grant table or an empty list of operations count as allowed. Absence of a rule is not permission.
items.reflection: Think of a rule at work or home that defaults to yes. What would change if it defaulted to no and you had to list what is allowed?

items.prompt: Implement `canAccessAll(grants, role, table, operations)`. Return `true` only if the role holds EVERY listed operation on the table. An empty `operations` list asks for nothing specific, so return `false`.
items.explanation: Every requested operation must be held, which is what every does. The empty-list guard matters because every on an empty list is vacuously true, and that would turn an empty request into an allow.
items.reference:
Default-deny, written down
unknown role: deny
unlisted table: deny
listed table, wrong operation: deny
only an exact role, table, and operation match allows
Why: a forgotten rule then fails closed instead of open.

items.prompt: Implement `allowedTables(grants, role, operation)`. Return an array, sorted alphabetically, of the tables on which the role holds the operation. An unknown role returns `[]`.
items.explanation: A missing role becomes an empty object, so no tables are returned. Filtering by the exact operation keeps the answer to what is actually granted, and sorting makes the order predictable.

items.prompt: Implement `firstDenied(grants, role, requests)`. `requests` is a list of `{ table, operation }`. Return the index of the first request the role is NOT allowed to make, or `-1` if every request is allowed. An unknown role is denied at index 0.

tests.expr: expect(firstDenied({ svc: { orders: ["SELECT"], products: ["SELECT"] } }, "svc", [{ table: "orders", operation: "SELECT" }, { table: "products", operation: "SELECT" }])).toBe(-1)
expect(firstDenied({ svc: { orders: ["SELECT"] } }, "svc", [{ table: "orders", operation: "SELECT" }, { table: "payments", operation: "SELECT" }])).toBe(1)

items.explanation: findIndex returns the first request whose check fails closed, or -1 when none does. An unknown role fails the very first check, so the answer is index 0.
